 1h ago WICKET! England 180-7 (Cox c Davies b Meredith 27) 
 1h ago WICKET! England 150-6 (Curran c Shaw b Chaudhary 21) 
 1h ago WICKET! England 123-5 (Jacks LBW b Zampa 3) 
 2h ago WICKET! England 117-4 (Banton c Shaw b Dwarshuis 39) 
 2h ago WICKET! England 110-3 (Brook c Harper b Chaudhary 65)

 1m ago 05.33 EST 6th over: Australia 53-2 (Marsh 18, Chaudhary 0) “I fully endorse your view that Dawson should’ve had 40 or 50 Test caps to his name by now,” writes James Matthews. “Has it ever been fathomed why the England management has so steadfastly ignored him for a series of spinners with ‘metrics’ and ‘potential’ in their favour, but little else? He has the spinner’s biggest weapon in spades: the ability to draw the batter into a stroke he doesn’t really want to play. England’s Test side has been calling out for a ‘control’ spinner ever since Leach was jettisoned.”
 That probably needs an essay, too, as it’s a complicated case. Lotta ins, lotta outs, lotta what-have-yous. My biggest frustration is that they binned him after one poor performance at Old Trafford last year, a game that bore precisely bugger all resemblance to what was going to happen in Australia. That said, I understand why they invested in Shoaib Bashir given his height and how well he bowled against India in his debut series.
 I promise I’ll get over the 2025-26 Ashes, one of these decades.
 Share 2m ago 05.32 EST WICKET! Australia 53-2 (Harper c Jacks b Crocombe 32)
 Henry Crocombe takes his first T20I wicket. Harper, who uppercut thrillingly for six earlier in the over, blasted a slower ball miles in the air and was taken at point by Jacks. That was a charming cameo on debut from Harper: 32 from 15 balls with three fours and two sixes.
 Share 8m ago 05.27 EST 5th over: Australia 42-1 (Marsh 17, Harper 23) On comes Sam Curran, who loved the MCG dimensions during the 2022 T20 World Cup. Marsh violates his first ball down the ground for four, then survives a Spandex-tight run-out referral after a direct hit from Overton at mid-on.
 England thought it was out; so did Marsh, who took his gloves off and was in the process of doing one when the replay showed he had just made his ground. It’s Shadab Khan all over again.
 Five from the over, a very good comeback from Curran after a boundary first ball.
 “Look, Rob,” begins Ian Copestake, “we know you like a joke as much as a stat about how many pastries the Aussies consumed in the lunch break of the 1984 Test in Adelaide against the Windies. But c’mon, what is Jake Fraser-McGurk’s real name?”
 Erm, Jake Matthew Fraser-McGurk?
 Share 13m ago 05.22 EST 4th over: Australia 37-1 (Marsh 12, Harper 23) Jamie Overton’s first over disappears for 21! Twenty of them came from the bat of the local boy Sam Harper. He edged four, top-edged just short of the diving Donald, slashed a more deliberate four through backwrd point, scooped an outrageous six and then flashed another boundary past the keeper Jordan Cox. Welcome to international cricket.
 View image in fullscreen Sam Harper hits out. Photograph: James Ross/AAP Share Updated at  05.27 EST 18m ago 05.16 EST 3rd over: Australia 16-1 (Marsh 12, Harper 3) Harper works Dawson off the pads for two, his first runs in international cricket. Another good over from Dawson, though – four from it.
 Share 20m ago 05.15 EST 2nd over: Australia 11-1 (Marsh 10, Harper 0) Marsh welcomes Henry Crocombe to T20Is by pulling his first ball over backward square leg for six. Marsh is extraordinarily good on the pull, a shot he played repeatedly during one of the great forgotten innings: 118 from 118 balls at Headingley during the 2023 Ashes. That knock deserves a Phil Walker essay.
 Crocombe holds his nerve, adjusts his line and length, and concedes only three from the last five balls of the over. That’s a good comeback.
 “Substack?” sniffs Ian Copestake. “Bleh. Is like those cameras with phones on them. I mean who wants that?!”
 Share 24m ago 05.10 EST 1st over: Australia 3-1 (Marsh 2, Harper 0) A terrific first over from Dawson. The new batter is the debutant Sam Harper.
 “Didn’t realise you weren’t well,” writes Felix Wood. “Sorry to hear and very glad you’re back on your feet, and selfishly that you’re back on OBO duty. You’re the best in the business.”
 Stop it now. (Don’t stop it. But please do know how touched and grateful I am.)
 Share 25m ago 05.09 EST WICKET! Australia 3-1 (Fraser-McGurk b Dawson 1)
 Canny is as canny does. Dawson sees – or senses – Fraser-McGurk coming down the track, holds the ball back and beats him all ends up. Fraser-McGurk says goodnight to his stumps and keeps walking. Experience 1-0 Youth.
 View image in fullscreen Jake Fraser-McGurk of Australia is bowled by Dawson. Photograph: Quinn Rooney/Getty Images Share Updated at  05.20 EST 28m ago 05.06 EST Liam Dawson , a canny left-arm spinner who should have played 40 Tests including four or five in Australia last winter but let’s not get into that now, will open the bowling.
 Share 31m ago 05.04 EST Time for the runchase. We say it every time, but Mitch Marsh is a key man. He’s opening the batting with Jake Fraser-McGurk.
 Share 32m ago 05.03 EST Hey, I’ve found a great new platform that lets writers, podcasters and video creators share work directly with subscribers. It’s called Substack – that name will never catch on – and I’ll be writing on there about cricket, football and maybe mental health. Please subscribe !
 Share 35m ago 04.59 EST A reminder of the latest sandpaper news 
 Pat Cummins to remain Test captain despite intense pressure amid sandpapergate scandal Read more Share 45m ago 04.49 EST Harry Brook has just given a pair of gloves to a young fan who was hit by one of his sixes. He’s being interviewed by Adam Gilchrist on the TV coverage.
 double quotation mark I feel like we’ve got a good score. Hopefully we can use the dimensions of the ground to our advantage.
 I moved around a lot, mainly to try to put the ball bowlers, but I’m still playing the ball on instinct. I’m literally trying to see the balla and hit the ball.
 Gilly would surely approve of that last line.
 Share 47m ago 04.48 EST Australia need 188 to win
 20th over: England 187-9 (Rashid 0) A fabulous last over from Jack Edwards – no boundaries, one wicket, one bye and only four runs off the bat.
 Cracking fightback from Australia, who were in all sorts when England were 104-2 after eight overs.
 Share 48m ago 04.47 EST WICKET! England 187-9 (Dawson run out 17)
 Dawson is run out off the final delivery after turning for a non-existent second just in case there was a misfield.
 Share 50m ago 04.44 EST WICKET! England 185-8 (Overton b Edwards 2)
 Overton is dropped by Tim David, a very tough low chanve at long-on. That’s at least six chances that have gone down. In thise case, no matter: Edwards cleans him up with a quite beautiful slower yorker. That was nigh-on perfect.
 Two balls remaining.
 View image in fullscreen Overton out, bowled by a yorker from Jack Edwards. Photograph: James Ross/AAP Share Updated at  05.01 EST 54m ago 04.41 EST 19th over: England 181-7 (Dawson 13, Overton 1) The new batter Jamie Overton cloths a hook straight up in the air. Somehow it lands safely.
 The highest successful chase in a T20 international at the MCG is Sri Lanka’s 172 for 5 in 2017.
 “I took my time to be convinced by Jordan Cox, but he’s a gem of a cricketer, isn’t he?” writes James Matthews. “Always bats unselfishly and so often adds impetus towards the end of the batting effort. Him and Jacks in the middle order give England wonderful balance and their big guns up the order licence to go hard at every ball, safe in the knowledge that there is genuine depth right down the order.
 “And as I type, he holes out. I stand by my point, yeronner.”
 Yeah, I was the same. I was think I was spooked when he was bounced out by Alzarri in that ODI series in the Caribbean two years ago, but there is so much to like about him. And batters are allowed to improve against the short ball: contrast Jonny Bairstow v Kemar Roach in 2012 and then v New Zealand in 2022.
 Share Updated at  04.42 EST 1h ago 04.39 EST WICKET! England 180-7 (Cox c Davies b Meredith 27)
 A useful cameo from Cox, 27 from 20 balls, ends with a roundhouse pull that is nicely taken on the run at deep midwicket.
 Australia are facing a record target on this ground, yet they’ve still done well to pull this back. At one stage England were eyeing 250.
 Share 1h ago 04.36 EST 18th over: England 175-6 (Cox 23, Dawson 12) Zampa’s final over goes for 11. First Dawson lifts an elegantly boundary over wide mid-on, then Cox picks the gap to the left of mid- off .
 It would have been 15 from the over had a fierce blow from Cox not hit the non-striker Dawson. Two overs to go.
 “Very glad to hear of your recovery – hope you’re ok,” writes James Brough. “Every so often, you find something that highlights how the game has changed. When I started watching cricket, David Gower was England’s premier batsman. I looked up his career stats for something a few days ago. Test career – 10 sixes in 117 games. Harry Brook just hit six sixes in about 20 minutes...”
 View image in fullscreen Jordan Cox dives to make his ground. Photograph: Asanka Brendon Ratnayake/AP Share Updated at  04.39 EST 1h ago 04.33 EST 17th over: England 164-6 (Cox 18, Dawson 6) Cox survives a run-out referral after turning Davies into the leg side and coming back from a second. He had to scramble desperately to make his ground, but did so successfully. Like vibes, dives matter.
 Cox celebrates his reprieve by dumping a reverse sweep over the top for four.
 “Hi Rob,” says Gary Naylor. “Lovely to have you back. I recognise that feeling you describe with ‘the surge of joie de vivre you get after serious illness’ not through poor health (so far) but from near-misses on the motorbike. The thrill was such that I’d never felt so alive. So, do batters get that same rush after a successful DRS review? Maybe they have enough joie de vivre.”
 Maybe they get it while facing extreme pace? Robin Smith certainly loved the sensation of a 90mph bouncer whooshing past his nose.
 Share 1h ago 04.27 EST 16th over: England 155-6 (Cox 11, Dawson 4) The legspinner Nikhil Chaudhary, playing only his fourth T20 international, finishes a game-changing spell with superb figures of 4-0-21-2. He conceded only one boundary, and even that was a false stroke from Tom Banton.
 Share 1h ago 04.24 EST WICKET! England 150-6 (Curran c Shaw b Chaudhary 21)
 That last entry aged well. Curran slices the first ball of Chaudhary’s final over to Shaw, who takes a good catch running in from the cover boundary.
 Curran goes for 21 from 21 balls; that will annoy him more than a single-figure dismissal.
 View image in fullscreen Australia's Lachie Shaw takes the catch to dismiss Dawson. Photograph: Asanka Brendon Ratnayake/AP Share Updated at  04.28 EST 1h ago 04.23 EST 15th over: England 150-5 (Curran 21, Cox 10) This situation is perfect for Curran, who is a much better T20 player when he has a bit of time to get his eye in. He has 21 from 19 balls, while Cox – who ends Riley Meredith’s over by deflecting a low full toss for four – is 10 from 10.
 Share Updated at  04.23 EST 1h ago 04.18 EST 14th over: England 141-5 (Curran 17, Cox 5) Curran rifles Zampa down the ground for four, the first boundary since the ninth over. Cracking shot. Even after a mid-innings lull, England are scoring at ten an over.
 Share 1h ago 04.15 EST 13th over: England 133-5 (Curran 11, Cox 3) Chaudhary continues the fightback that he started with the wicket of Brook. Six from the over, none in boundaries.
 This has been an innings of three-thirds
 First 3 overs 18-2
 Next 5 overs 86-0
 Last 5 overs 29-3
 Share 1h ago 04.12 EST 12th over: England 127-5 (Curran 6, Cox 2) England bat deep, with Jordan Cox coming in at No7. This pair can afford to take two or three overs to rebuild. That allows Zampa to zip through the remainder of his second over while conceding only four singles.
 “Intrigued by the TV graphic showing the quality of bat contact as percentages of ‘smoked’ or ‘muscled’, with Harry Brook’s angled six to third man ranking 100% smoked and a brutal midwicket missile only 67% muscled,” writes Brian Withington. “Not quite sure how this is measured and what HB’s glide into the keeper’s gloves would have registered as?”
 92% dog’s-dinnered? 100% cagged?
 Share Updated at  05.00 EST 1h ago 04.09 EST WICKET! England 123-5 (Jacks LBW b Zampa 3)
 Jacks plays defensively around a legbreak from Zampa and is hit on the pad in front of leg stump. The finger goes up, Jacks’ review is unsuccessful and ENGLAND ARE COLLAPSING IN AUSTRALIA AGAIN SEND THEM HOME FFS England have lost three wickets for 13. Three big ones, too: Brook, Banton and Jacks.
 Share 1h ago 04.05 EST 11th over: England 123-4 (Curran 3, Jacks 4) Four from Chaudhary’s over. In context, his figures of 2-0-10-1 are seriously good. Seriously serious.
 Share 2h ago 04.04 EST 10th over: England 119-4 (Curran 1, Jacks 2) “Hi Rob,” says Simon McMahon. “Sorry, not been as up to date with the blogs recently, I had no idea you’d been unwell, sounds scary, glad to hear you’re on the mend. Let’s leave it to England for any collapses from now on, eh. Take it easy.”
 That’s the plan.
 View image in fullscreen Take her easy, Dude. Photograph: BFA/Alamy Share 2h ago 04.01 EST WICKET! England 117-4 (Banton c Shaw b Dwarshuis 39)
 Is it a bird? Is it a plane? No, it’s Lachlan Bloody Shaw! He has just taken a spectacular diving catch to get rid of Tom Banton, a delightful moment for a kid making his international debut. Banton walloped Dwarshuis flat and hard towards deep square leg, where Shaw ran round the boundary and swooped elegantly to his right to take the catch. Lovely stuff.
 Share 2h ago 03.58 EST 9th over: England 110-3 (Banton 34, Curran 0) That was another barnstorming innings from Brook: 65 from 28 balls with four fours and six sixes. In his last six T20 internationals – yes, that’s an entirely gratuitous sample size – Brook has an average of 136 and a strike rate of 220.
 “Following along the OBO and great to see another fresh-faced bowler joining our ranks,” says Will Brookes. “If Henry Crocombe’s nickname isn’t Boosh then can we start a petition to change it? Niche baking references make the best nicknames.”
 Tell that to ‘One Size’ Fitz Hall.
 Share 2h ago 03.56 EST WICKET! England 110-3 (Brook c Harper b Chaudhary 65)
 Well bowled Nikhil Chaudhary! An excellent first over ends with the vital wicket of Brook, who tries to glide the ball for four but gets it too fine and is smartly caught by the debutant Harper.
 View image in fullscreen Sam Harper takes a smart catch to dismiss Harry Brook. Photograph: Quinn Rooney/Getty Images Share Updated at  04.06 EST 2h ago 03.53 EST Banton is not out It was pad.
 Share 2h ago 03.53 EST Australia review for caught behind against Banton On comes the legspinner Nikhil Chaudhary. Australia review for a leg-side catch when Banton works across the line. It hit something, pad or bat. We’re about to find out which.
 Share 2h ago 03.51 EST 8th over: England 104-2 (Brook 64, Banton 29) Adam Zampa’s first ball is dumped behind square for four by Banton. His third ball is a lamentable – nay, despicable – long hop that Brook hoicks into the crowd at backward square leg. He has 64 from 26 balls, including 57 from the last 17.
 Banton completes another big over with consecutive boundaries, a reverse-sweep over short third and a sadistic thwack down the ground. Try explaining that sentence to a Martian.
 England have scored 86 in the last five overs. 
 Share 2h ago 03.48 EST 7th over: England 84-2 (Brook 57, Banton 16) Dropped catch No5. Banton clubs Davies to long on, where the usually reliable Tim David spills an awkward running catch. He would take that maybe eight times out of 10. On this occasion, it’s four runs to Banton.
 “It seems giving Harry Brook three chances to build an innings is a rather colossal mistake,” says James Matthews. “Who knew? Penny for Adam Zampa’s thoughts right now.”
 Give it a few years and Meta should have the necessary technology. It’ll cost a lot more than a penny, mind.
 Share 2h ago 03.44 EST Brook charges to 20-ball fifty!
 6th over: England 74-2 (Brook 53, Banton 10) Edwards has a big LBW shout turned down when Banton misses a heave at a slower ball. That looks really close, but Australia decide not review.
 Good lord, Brook’s at it again. He launches Edwards into the crowd at midwicket, his fifth sixth in the last 10 balls. A ferocious four down the ground brings up a stunning fifty to 20 balls; that includes 45 runs from the last 11 deliveries . If only England produced players of such unfettered genius.
 Banton clears the leaping fielder at long on, just, for his first six. Mercy.
 Share Updated at  04.13 EST 2h ago 03.40 EST 5th over: England 56-2 (Brook 42, Banton 4) The fourth dropped catch in five overs. Banton smokes the ball back at Ben Dwarshuis, who can’t take a very difficult chance in his follow through. A tenth of a chance at best.
 Four dropped catches – and now four sixes for Harry Brook, who slams a short ball from Dwarshuis over midwicket with disdain. What a player! He touches the parts that no England player since Kevin Pietersen has reached.
 View image in fullscreen Harry Brook punishing Australia. Photograph: Quinn Rooney/Getty Images Share Updated at  03.45 EST 2h ago 03.37 EST Brook smashes 24 off Meredith over
 4th over: England 42-2 (Brook 30, Banton 2) It’s unadvisable to give Harry Brook one life, never mind two. He punishes Australia – and demonstrates his sheer genius – by hitting Meredith for three sixes in a row.
 First he jumped inside the line to help a short ball round the corner. The next delivery was pretty much in the same spot, but this time Brook leaned back to uppercut it over the slips.
 He charged the next ball, pulling it violently over midwicket, then threaded four past extra cover. Oh, the audacity!
 Twenty-four from the over, and in the blink of an eye Brook is 30 not out from 14 balls.
 “England’s batters are in the image of their coach and, I suspect, will continue to play a shot a ball until they run out of batters,” says James Matthews. “However, it’s worth looking at the other side of the fence: Australia have bowled superbly; mixing up pace and line to prevent the batters getting any sort of rhythm. If only their catching was up to the quality of their bowling, they’d have this game in the bag already.”
 Share Updated at  03.38 EST 2h ago 03.32 EST 3rd over: England 18-2 (Brook 7, Banton 1) Blimey, Brook has been dropped again! This is bizarre. He whirled Edwards to short third, where Zampa got in a pickle and helped the ball over his left shoulder to the boundary. That was the easiest chance of the three that have been put down.
 We know Brendon McCullum’s England like to run towards the danger. At the moment they’re re-enacting the final scene of Blackadder Goes Forth.
 Share 2h ago 03.28 EST WICKET! England 13-2 (Donald c Marsh b Edwards 10)
 Nye Donald’s manic cameo is over. He clubbed Jack Edwards’ first ball high in the air to mid-off, a poor stroke to a back-of-a-length delivery that cramped him for room. Donald can clearly play, but in his short international career he’s been a bit too frantic.
 Share 2h ago 03.26 EST 2nd over: England 13-1 (Donald 10, Brook 3) Now Brook has been dropped ! He beasted Riley Meredith’s first ball to backward point, where Jake Fraser-McGurk put down a sharp but relatively straightforward chance.
 Donald pulls England’s first boundary, then edges another through the right hand of the debutant keeper Harper. That’s another dropped catch ! Harper was slightly slow to spring to his right, though it was still a pretty tough chance.
 “Following the OBO, sorry to hear you’ve not been so good,” writes Derek Walmsley. “I’ve been reading your stuff for, what, 20 odd years and always enjoy seeing your byline. Long may it continue, like a Hashim Amla ton on a sunny weekend.”
 Ah, thanks Derek. Not sure I have a gazillionth of Hashim Amla’s serenity, but I’ll take it – even if it does evoke that painful, end-of-an-era Saturday at The Oval in 2012 .
 Share 2h ago 03.20 EST 1st over: England 2-1 (Donald 1, Brook 1) Harry Brook had a poor ODI series with the bat, but his recent T20 form has been outrageous.
 He gets off the mark with a single, then Donald is fortunate to see a couple of errant sweeps land safely. England have started like a moggy on a hot tin roof.
 Share 2h ago 03.17 EST WICKET! England 0-1 (Salt c Marsh b Davies 0)
 Joel Davies strikes first ball! Phil Salt, who can struggle against left-arm spin, smashed a full ball straight to mid-off, where Mitchell Marsh took the catch at the second attempt. Yikes.
 View image in fullscreen Salt exits the field. Photograph: James Ross/AAP Share Updated at  03.33 EST 2h ago 03.16 EST Time for the action. England have an all-Welsh opening partnership of Phil Salt and Nye Donald. Apparently it’s the first time since 2000 that two Welshmen have played for England. Robert Croft and …?
 Share Updated at  03.16 EST 3h ago 03.03 EST I’m off to score some Colombian (coffee, your honour), but will be back in time for the first ball of the series.
 Share 3h ago 03.03 EST “Very sorry to read during the ODI that you’ve been unwell,” writes Robert Ellson. “Hope you’re recovering well. Enjoy the game.”
 Ah, thanks Robert, and thanks to all of you who sent such kind messages. The rest of you can go to hell. They really do mean a lot. It was pretty hairy for 36 hours, and I wouldn’t wish the experience on [insert name of despot here], but I survived thanks to remarkably kind people.
 I’m fine now and revelling in the surge of joie de vivre you get after serious illness. I was going to say I’m mad for it, but let’s not get carried away; at heart I’m still a craggy quinquagenarian.
 View image in fullscreen Mad f’rit. Photograph: Des Willie/Redferns Share Updated at  03.07 EST 3h ago 02.58 EST Team news
 Australia have two debutants of their own: Lechlan Shaw , 23, and Sam Harper , 29, will wear the Baggy Green for the first time.
 England also have a late bloomer on whom you are advised to keep an eye: the opener Nye Donald has a T20 strike rate of 173, and in the last couple of years it’s in excess of 200. Blink and you might miss him.
 Adil Rashid returns to the white-ball side and will play in tandem with Liam Dawson.
 Australia Marsh (c), Fraser-McGurk, Harper (wk), David, Shaw, Edwards, Chaudhary, Davies, Dwarshuis, Meredith, Zampa.
 England Salt, Donald, Brook (c), Cox (wk), Banton, Jacks, Curran, Overton, Dawson, Rashid, Crocombe.
 Share Updated at  03.05 EST 3h ago 02.51 EST Australia win the toss and bowl
 And why not? Harry Brook says England would have batted anyway.
 Share Updated at  03.03 EST 3h ago 02.51 EST Henry Crocombe has been handed a piece of headgear by his new Surrey team-mate Sam Curran, which means he’ll be making his T20 international debut. Against Australia. At the G .
 The other thing to note is that the cap’s traditional panelled construction and adjustable strap ensure a comfortable fit, while vent holes promote airflow for breathability.
 View image in fullscreen Henry Crocombe is presented with his England cap. Photograph: William West/AFP/Getty Images Share Updated at  03.06 EST 3h ago 02.35 EST In other news, India are dominating the first Test against New Zealand in Wellington. They finished day three on 486 for 4, a lead of 118, with their top five all passing fifty. KL Rahul, elegance incarnate, top-scored with a patient 136. How the hell does that man have a Test average in the 30s? 
 The Spin | Why is KL Rahul’s average so low? Here are some explanations Read more Share Updated at  02.36 EST 3h ago 02.27 EST Jonathan Horn Who ssaid long-form journalism is dead ? As Matt Renshaw nudged his ones and twos in an already forgotten ODI match, the broadcasters were scanning Cameron Bancroft’s 4000-word essay . SEN’s Gerard Whateley was calling for a comprehensive judicial inquiry, “a little bit like a coroner’s inquest,” with witnesses compelled to attend and be subjected to cross examination. Cricket Australia’s “forum” , announced a few hours earlier, had already been skittled.
 Nothing in the eight years since a piece of sandpaper was taken on to the field in Cape Town, including the publication of Usman Khawaja’s book Sabr , had been as revelatory as Bancroft’s first-person account . But as always with this story, we were bracing for the next press conference, the next podcast, the next corroborating statement, the next counterclaim, the next overreaction.
 For many, and certainly for Pat Cummins, his press conference less than a week earlier was supposed to be the final word . Some cricketers write books, some pen essays, and some post videos from the foot of the Himalayas . Some people crumble in front of the baying pack, and some relish it.
 Sandpapergate has gone from a sporting scandal to a rolling loop of outrage and overreaction | Jonathan Horn Read more Share Updated at  02.56 EST 3h ago 02.09 EST Ali Martin After a toe-curling, stonewalling press conference before the recent one-day series against England , Australia’s usually happy-go-lucky T20 captain, Mitch Marsh, opted out of a repeat before the Twenty20s that start here on Saturday.
 In his place came Victoria’s Sam Harper to talk about his looming debut at the MCG. A nice local angle, for sure, with the 29-year-old wicketkeeper having overcome some troubling concussions in the past.  Mike Hytner Cricket Australia has thrown its “unanimous” support behind embattled Test captain Pat Cummins, saying the bowler will continue in his leadership role despite the intense pressure on him after the sandpapergate controversy resurfaced in recent weeks.
 Cummins’ position as captain had been called into question after the publication of Usman Khawaja’s memoir, in which the former Australia opener claimed the entire team knew of the plot to tamper with the ball on the tour of South Africa in 2018.
 But after the CA chair, David Boon, and the CEO, Todd Greenberg, met with Cummins in Sydney on Friday, they gave him their full backing in a statement on Saturday.
 “We’ve expressed our support to Pat and our concern for everyone impacted by the events of the 2018 tour of South Africa,” Boon said.
 “We have learned from that experience and are proud of the team and the culture Pat and other leaders in the team have fostered over the past eight years and unequivocally reject any implication that Pat’s integrity has been compromised.”

 Rob Smyth We interrupt the sandpaper news cycle to bring you some live cricket: Australia v England at the MCG, the first in a five-match T20 series. It’s two years until the next T20 World Cup, so the contextometer isn’t exactly zinging, but this should be a fun contest between the teams who are third and first in the ICC rankings.
 England’s recent T20 form puts the ‘cor’ in ‘coruscating’: they’ve won 23 out of 26 completed games since Harry Brook became full-time captain, and put the world champions India across their knee during the English summer.
 Australia’s annus has been a little more horribilis. They lost 3-0 in Pakistan and left no trace at the T20 World Cup. A 3-0 win over Bangladesh in June provided a soupçon of hope for the future, particularly a World Cup on home soil in 2028. Victory over England would be a good way to build on that.
